definition: Overstated means put more strongly than the facts support — described as bigger, better, or worse than it really is.
task: Write one sentence of your own using the word overstated. Make the sentence show what the word means -- a reader who did not know overstated should be able to work it out from your sentence.
avoid_verbatim: The brochure's promise of 'sweeping ocean views' proved overstated: from the balcony you could see a gray sliver of harbor between two parking garages.
Slanted is milder than overstated: a slanted account tilts emphasis and word choice while keeping the numbers honest, whereas an overstated one pushes the claim itself past what the facts support.
Baseless goes further than overstated: an overstated danger is a real danger described too strongly, while a baseless one has no fact beneath it at all.

Overblown is exaggeration past all proportion — overblown praise, overblown fears, overblown prose. Overstated is the cooler, auditor's verdict: a specific claim or figure pitched above what the evidence supports, usually by someone who expects to be believed.

Oversold is a promoter's failing: a product or idea pitched as more than it is. Overstated points at the claim itself rather than the sales pitch — a risk, a benefit, or a number can be overstated in a report nobody is trying to sell.
matching the facts exactly, neither more nor less
careful and restrained, claiming no more than the evidence allows

When the district announced that its new reading program had 'transformed' test scores, the auditors found the claim overstated: scores had indeed risen, but by four points, not the forty the press release implied.
Overstated is the exact word because the gain was real and only its size was pushed past the evidence.
A false claim has no fact beneath it; an overstated one takes a genuine fact and pitches it too high.
The auditors' quarrel is with the volume of the claim, not its existence.
Overstated is the reviewer's and auditor's word: it concedes that something real is there and objects only that the claim outruns it.
If the speaker knows the stretch and expects you to smile rather than believe, that is hyperbole, taught in this same unit; if nothing real sits under the claim at all, the word is false.
Overstated keeps the argument about degree.

When the district unveiled its renovated gym, the press release called it 'a facility doubling the space available to student athletes.' The student paper's editors measured.
The new weight room and mezzanine brought the gain to about forty percent — generous, but well short of the claim.
Their story was careful to be fair: the renovation was real, the improvements substantial, the coaches genuinely pleased.
But the headline figure, they wrote, had been overstated — the space had grown, just not doubled.
The superintendent conceded the point in a letter, thanking them for checking the number instead of repeating it.
